listings.name: qxmagazine.com
listings.content: A weekly magazine that comprehensively covers the London gay scene with handy night by night listings available on-line and in print

listings.name: Boyz Magazine
listings.content: Which is published fortnightly and is freely available at most London gay venues, and contains listings of everything that is happening in all the major clubs in London and the South East.

listings.name: British Museum
listings.content: A vast repository of the world's cultures, controversially including hundreds of items that were looted from their places of origin. Entire sections are devoted to Egyptian, Greek, and Middle Eastern artifacts, as well as the piece which united them all, the Rosetta Stone. Other items on everyone's list are the largest collection of mummies outside Egypt and the Elgin Marbles. The collection also includes some of the world's finest collections of Chinese and Sub-Saharan African art; perhaps the most famous of the latter are the Benin bronzes. A definite highlight of a trip to London. Temporary exhibitions are invariably excellent and meticulously researched, but can be expensive. It has a fine store, mainly selling replicas of items in the collection.

listings.name: Cartoon Museum
listings.content: A vast collection of cartoons and comics on display with special, often topical, exhibitions.

listings.name: Charles Dickens Museum
listings.content: Museum at the former home of Dickens exhibiting writings, paintings, furniture and other items relating to the writer.
listings.price: £5, students and seniors £4, children £3, families £14 (two adults and up to five children), special group rates apply

listings.name: Foundling Museum
listings.content: A museum and a gallery telling the story of the Foundling Hospital, an orphanage for abandoned children founded in the 18th century. Massive art donations by British artists and the involvement of George Friederic Handel as a patron made this childcare organisation an early centre of art and music.

listings.name: Fitzroy House
listings.content: A historic house that was inhabited by playwright George Bernard Shaw, it is where writer L. Ron Hubbard, founder of Scientology, worked in the 1950s. The building is reminiscent of the time, complete with Adler typewriters, Grundig tape recorders, and Western Union telefax. Tours by appointment.

listings.name: Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology
listings.content: Formerly the teaching collection of Sir Flinders Petrie, one of Britain's greatest archaeologists, now preserved by University College London. Exhibits include beaded dresses, sculpture and wall reliefs, items of everyday use, papyri, cartonnage and pottery. Fascinating!

listings.name: Pollock's Toy Museum
listings.content: A treasure trove of antique toys exhibited in a warren of 6 rooms above the toy shop of the same name. A very charming place indeed, though the doll rooms are a bit gruesome.

listings.name: Wellcome Collection
listings.content: Sir Henry Solomon Wellcome's vast collection of medical artefacts and art work that together explore what it means to be human. Special health related exhibitions.

listings.name: Camera Museum
listings.content: A downstairs museum dedicated to cameras from the 1800s to present day, including a camera rifle like the one used in Licence to Kill. The museum is a quick visit and worth the stop even for someone with a moderate interest in photography.

listings.name: Brunei Gallery, SOAS University of London
listings.content: An exhibition space that hosts a programme of changing contemporary and historical exhibitions from Asia, Africa and the Middle East, aiming to present and promote cultures from these regions and to be a student resource and public facility. There are live music performances every last Wednesday of every month except December and July.

listings.name: All Saints, Margaret Street
listings.content: An attractive Gothic Revival church, completed in 1859 to a design by William Butterfield.

listings.name: All Souls Church, Langham Place
listings.content: Completed in 1823, this attractive church near Broadcasting House is one of John Nash's masterpieces, with a prominent spire and circular vestibule. As of May 2025, it accessible only for worship.

listings.name: Bedford Square
listings.content: This wonderful square was built between 1775 and 1783 as an upper middle class residential area takes its name from the Dukes of Bedford, who were the main landlords in Bloomsbury. Distinguished residents have included Lord Eldon, one of Britain's longest serving and most celebrated Lord Chancellors. This is one of the best preserved set pieces of Georgian architecture in London and the majority of the buildings are grade I listed. The gardens are private and always remain locked - there are no 'open days'.

listings.name: British Telecom Tower
listings.content: 191-m (627-ft) skyscraper can be seen from far away and is the sixth highest building in UK.

listings.name: Bloomsbury Square
listings.content: This garden square was established by Lord Southampton in 1665 and is the oldest square in London. It was opened to the public in the 1950s. The square is surrounded by a number of beautiful 18th- and 19th-century buildings and terraces.

listings.name: Coram's Fields
listings.content: A park which is run as children's play area. Facilities include a pet's corner, lawns, sports pitches and a nursery. No adults are allowed to enter the park unless they are accompanying children. All visitors are welcome to join the local kids.

listings.name: Russell Square
listings.content: The largest square in London. It was established in 1806 by the 5th Duke of Bedford and his statue can still be seen in the square. There is also a café.

listings.name: Senate House Building
listings.content: Art deco headquarters of University of London featured in the film Nineteen Eighty-Four.

listings.name: St George's Gardens
listings.content: Peaceful gardens and interesting monuments including the daughter of Richard Cromwell, son of Oliver Cromwell.

listings.name: Goodenough College
listings.content: Goodenough College offers accommodation for international postgraduate students. The college's student community of approx 650 represents over 90 countries, offering a unique experience through stimulating intellectual debate, fostering cross-cultural activity and providing an exceptional social environment. Tours around the college are offered every Friday at 1PM and every first Saturday of the month at 11AM.

listings.name: University College London
listings.content: Includes a small but beautiful quad and an interesting Neo-Classical facade. The core buildings of UCL were built after the university's foundation in 1826.

listings.name: BBC Broadcasting House
listings.content: The complex incorporates the Old Broad House built in 1930s. The façades of which feature the famous sculpture of Prospero and Ariel and the Ariel friezes by Eric Gill and Gilbert Bayes. BBC's The One Show is transmitted from the studio at the ground floor every weeknight starting from 7PM. The studio is quite visible from the plaza outside and some parts of the show are performed from outside of the studio – in the plaza.

listings.name: Birkbeck Institute for the Moving Image
listings.content: Cinema owned by Birkbeck, University of London, featuring screenings and lectures. Most events are free but pre-booking is advised.
listings.address: 43 Gordon Sq, Birkbeck, University of London, WC1H 0PD

listings.name: Bloomsbury Theatre
listings.content: Theatre owned by University College London staging both student and professional productions. Broad range of performances.

listings.name: Dominion Theatre
listings.content: A large London theatre that tends to show mainstream blockbuster-type musical productions.

listings.name: London Mathematical Society
listings.content: Based on Russell Square, they give lectures and exhibitions, for those numerically inclined.
listings.address: De Morgan House, 57-58 Russell Square, WC1B 4HS

listings.name: Curzon Bloomsbury
listings.content: Cinema showing arthouse and foreign language films.

listings.name: Walks
listings.content: Bloomsbury has a number of famous walks that cover the lives and works of the Bloomsbury Group.

listings.name: Bloomsbury Festival
listings.content: Takes place in the Summer around the environs of Bloomsbury, concentrated in Russell Square, and hosts arts and crafts fair, children's painting classes and dance workshops. The food stalls are good value too.

listings.name: Dal Fiorentino Fitzrovia
listings.content: A small sandwich shop away from the hustle and bustle of Fitzrovia that serves a quick lunch for under £10. Has meal deals! (updated Nov 2025)

listings.name: YouMeSushi
listings.content: Temporarily closed as of May 2022. Founded in 2008, YouMeSushi has gone from strength to strength with the opening of three additional venues. Eat in, take away or have sushi delivered straight to your door (within a 3-mile radius).

listings.name: Seoul Bakery
listings.content: Korean food.

listings.name: PaStation
listings.content: Italian cuisine.

listings.name: Cafe Metro Express
listings.content: Moroccan cuisine

listings.name: Siam Central
listings.content: A Thai restaurant

listings.name: Mary Ward Cafe
listings.content: Temporarily closed as of May 2022. A selection of veggie and vegan dishes that changes daily. Cakes, pastries, and salad available as well. Busy, eat in or take away.
listings.price: Under £5 for a heap of food

listings.name: Indian YMCA
listings.content: The hostel's restaurant is open to the public.

listings.name: Fish Bone
listings.content: Traditional fish 'n' chips restaurant.

listings.name: Attendant
listings.content: An independent coffee shop in a converted Victorian public toilet.

listings.name: Salaam Namaste
listings.content: Indian restaurant with dishes from around the country.

listings.name: Great Court Restaurant
listings.content: Housed in the British Museum, this restaurant offers a unique dining experience. For history buffs, it's the perfect setting to sit down and enjoy familiar favourites. Reservations recommended.
listings.address: The British Museum, Great Russell St, WC1B 3DG

listings.name: Mortimer House Kitchen
listings.content: Creative cuisine, starting from an Italian base, but with bigger plates and smaller, more exquisite food. Extremely friendly and helpful service. The small tables and easy chairs in front can serve as a bar or café if you don't want a meal.

listings.name: North Sea Fish
listings.content: Takeaway fish and chips next to a very popular fish restaurant that even serves Skate.

listings.name: Master Wei Xi'an
listings.content: Northern Chinese restaurant, specializing in authentic Xi'an dishes. Try the biangbiang noodles or the steamed dumplings.

listings.name: Elysee
listings.content: Greek restaurant fun to go to with plate smashing, music and belly dancing.

listings.name: Hakkasan
listings.content: Michelin-starred kitchen based on Cantonese tradition but also experimenting in other areas.

listings.name: Pied à Terre
listings.content: French restaurant with one Michelin star.

listings.name: Bubbledogs
listings.content: Champagne and cocktail bar serving gourmet hotdogs.

listings.name: Flying Horse
listings.content: A Grade 11 listed Nicolson's pub.

listings.name: The Wheatsheaf
listings.content: Freehouse with beautiful leaded windows. Used to be Aleister Crowley's regular.

listings.name: Sam Smith's Pubs
listings.content: Check also a map with pub locations.

listings.name: Fitzroy Tavern
listings.content: Owned by the Samuel Smith brewery, the Fitzroy Tavern offers good, cheap beer. The pub, which took its name from a local aristocrat, the Earl of Fitzroy, in turn inspired the name of the surrounding area of Bloomsbury, Fitzrovia, and was a popular drinking place for BBC broadcasters (including George Orwell) following the Second World War. A very friendly pub, with nice outdoor seating in summer.

listings.name: The College Arms
listings.content: Pub frequented by students from nearby University College London and Birkbeck College.

listings.name: The Jeremy Bentham
listings.content: Named after the prominent political philosopher and early supporter of University College London, and located very near the main entrance to the college, the pub tends to attract more senior academics than does the College Arms.

listings.name: The Lamb
listings.content: This beautifully preserved Victorian pub attracts many young and old patrons. Classic ales and some great food. Crowded after 5PM.

listings.name: The Lord John Russell
listings.content: Authentic pub popular with university students.

listings.name: The Museum Tavern
listings.content: A very good pub, offering a wide range of real ales, and some excellent food. Can get busy in the summer months.

listings.name: TCR Lounge Bar
listings.content: A common drinking place for medical students from University College Hospital, who jostle alongside office workers. Gets exceptionally crowded after office hours.

listings.name: Astor Museum Inn Hostel
listings.content: For 18-35 year-olds.

listings.name: Generator Hostels London
listings.content: Right in the heart of Bloomsbury. Communal showers and cold water, all-night parties and generally an architecture obviously designed exclusively with the easy clean-up of bodily fluids in mind. It is cheap, though, in London terms.

listings.name: YHA London Central
listings.content: The newest of the five London YHA hostels, with state-of-the-art interiors, and a short walk from Regent's Park.

listings.name: YHA London St Pancras
listings.content: The largest of the five London YHA hostels, minutes walk from St Pancras International railway station.

listings.name: UCL Summer Residences
listings.content: Student halls of residence which are made available for rental during academic holiday periods.

listings.name: Alhambra Hotel
listings.content: Well-known multi-lingual (Spanish, Portuguese, French) family hotel. Free wireless Internet.
listings.price: Single from £50, basic double £60, excellent English breakfast included

listings.name: The Apollo Hotel
listings.content: Clean, but staff somewhat unhelpful. WiFi Internet.
listings.price: Single from £48, basic double £58, English breakfast included

listings.name: Excelsior Hotel
listings.content: Budget hotel in a quiet, leafy square close to King's Cross Station. All rooms have high speed internet connection.

listings.name: Guilford House Hotel
listings.content: A little shabby but well-located and fair value.

listings.name: The Jesmond Dene Hotel
listings.content: A budget hotel run on a bed & breakfast basis. Free WiFi Internet access.

listings.name: Euston Square Hotel
listings.content: Completely renovated in 2008.

listings.name: Holiday Inn London Regents Park
listings.content: The hotel is near attractions including Madame Tussauds and has a restaurant and bar. It is also close to Tube and railway stations.

listings.name: George Hotel
listings.content: Historic building, full English breakfast.

listings.name: Goodenough Club
listings.content: 5 Georgian townhouses looking over the beautiful Mecklenburgh Square gardens. No lift.

listings.name: My Bloomsbury
listings.content: Funky and fashionable hotel with interiors by Conran and no surprise that it is listed in Hip Hotels.

listings.name: The Russell Hotel
listings.content: This Gothic building is a real landmark and dominates the eastern side of Russell Square. Not a cheap hotel by any means but good value for the location and standard. Popular with families. See the magnificent ballroom which was designed by the same people who created interiors for RMS Titanic.

listings.name: Sanderson Hotel
listings.content: Hotel features the Courtyard Garden, Jeffrey Chodorow’s Spoon restaurant, the Long Bar, the Purple Bar, Billiard Room, Agua Bathhouse, penthouse suites and multi-service meeting spaces.

listings.name: Charlotte Street Hotel
listings.content: Part of the upscale Firmdale chain, this is a lively stylish hotel close to British Museum. No dogs.

listings.name: British Library
listings.content: The official book depository of the United Kingdom, holding a copy of every book ever printed here, and a wide variety of periodicals. No less than 150 million items catalogued and there is an unimaginable 625 km of shelving! Visitors may not use the library unless they have proof of identity, home address, and a genuine need to use a specific item, but there is a free "Treasures of the British Library" exhibition chronicling the history of the written and printed word and displaying some of the library's best known items, including two of the original manuscripts of the Magna Carta and Leonardo Da Vinci's notebook. Additionally there are temporary exhibitions on historical or literary subjects, which charge admission. Popular ones can be very crowded at weekends. In the central atrium stands the King's Library (the library of King George III) surrounded by a glass wall, so visitors can occasionally see librarians retrieving books for readers. Tours of the library building run M W F-Su and cost £6. Call to book. Large items of luggage are not permitted in the building and cannot be stored in the cloakroom.

listings.name: Camley Street Natural Park
listings.content: A 2-acre nature reserve amid the industrial wasteland just north of King's Cross Station. This lovely little park gives visitors interested in nature the opportunity to learn about the work of the London Wildlife Trust who administer this and 26 other reserves in London. This is the only one in the centre of the city.

listings.name: Jewish Museum
listings.content: In 2010, it reopened after a renovation with a modern extension. Exhibitions on the long history of the Jewish community in London. Well laid out and interesting.
listings.price: Adult £7.50, senior (60+) or student or unemployed or disabled £5.50, child (5-16) £3.50, free with National Art Pass or London Pass of child under 5

listings.name: Regent's Canal
listings.content: You can walk or cycle along the canal through east London all the way to the Thames (3 hr). The St. Pancras lock is directly north of St Pancras station. Regent's Canal was once a lifeline for trade and industry in London with narrowboats and barges ferrying goods to and from North London. The canal winds its way from the Grand Union Canal near Paddington in West London, past Regent's Park, Camden, Islington and Mile End to Limehouse, where it meets the Thames. From Camden Lock you can walk upstream along the canal to Regent's Park and on to London Zoo. It is a great way to approach the Zoo and a good way to avoid the traffic. Downstream of Camden is less pretty but still an interesting walk, taking you through the Islington Tunnel (one of the longest tunnels in the British canal system) and out in to East London. Whichever way you go along the path, watch out for cyclists!

listings.name: St. Pancras Old Church and cemetery
listings.content: Hidden away behind St. Pancras railway station is what is believed to be one of the oldest sites of Christian worship in England. There has been a church on the site since at least around the year 314. The current church is mostly a 19th-century structure, but it contains some traces of an older Norman structure. Surrounding the church is a cemetery, today transformed into a public park that contains a memorial to philosopher and "mother of feminism" Mary Wollstonecraft, who was originally buried there before her remains were moved to Bournemouth. This is where her daughter Mary, the author of Frankenstein, first declared her love for her future husband, Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley.

listings.name: St. Pancras International railway station
listings.content: Ornate Neo-Gothic architecture, used in the Harry Potter films.

listings.name: Cecil Sharp House
listings.content: English Folk Dancing.
listings.address: 2 Regent's Park Rd, Primrose Hill, London NW1 7AY

listings.name: Shaw Theatre
listings.content: Theatre named after George Bernard Shaw and famous for showing high-quality non-mainstream productions.

listings.name: St. Pancras International Station
listings.content: A selection of cafes at the station. Convenient for a quick bite.

listings.name: Frida
listings.content: Mexican cafe bar & bistro with vegetarian & Vegan options.

listings.name: Ravi Shankar Bhelpoori House
listings.content: Indian restaurant named after the famous Indian sitarist and composer. A superb vegetarian Thali can be had for under £10. Wash it down with a Kingfisher and you are set for the night.

listings.name: The Devonshire Arms
listings.content: The dress code is strictly alternative and the pub has got a late night license for Fridays and Saturdays. DJs every night and some gigs. The artwork on the walls was produced by Robin, the barman.

listings.name: The Camden Road Draft House
listings.content: Victorian Boozer

listings.name: The Dublin Castle
listings.content: A bit rowdy and often quite packed, this pub and music venue has played a pivotal role in British music. It is well known for producing the 1980s band Madness and helping a great many other groups along their path to glory. Worth a stop, just for the atmosphere.

listings.name: The Edinboro Castle
listings.content: A more refined side of Camden, this pub is part of a chain in North London attempting to apply a little class. It has a fine selection of beer and cider, including a selection of Belgian beers both bottled and draught. The food is always good and the staff always friendly. There is a large, semi-covered outdoor seating area with heaters.

listings.name: The Good Mixer
listings.content: A nice pub where the likes of Blur and Pulp and a load of other Britpop bands from the 1990s used to drink. Prices are reasonable, there are two pool tables, and the general atmosphere is laid back and friendly.

listings.name: Hawley Arms
listings.content: Tucked away in a side street close to the Stables Market, this two-story pub has a small garden and a roof terrace. There are sometimes concerts upstairs. A favorite of the late Amy Winehouse.

listings.name: Jazz Café
listings.content: Food, drink, and music (jazz, soul, blues). Every Saturday the place turns into a great 1980s music club, with "I love the 80s".

listings.name: Waitrose's Wine Bar
listings.content: Pleasant and good-value place to sit and sip, though it closes when Waitrose around 9PM.

listings.name: The World's End
listings.content: Local landmark and a good meeting point. It is large, with two separate bars and a lot of seating. Food is served at the weekend.
listings.address: 174 Camden High St, Camden Town, NW1 0NE

listings.name: The Lion And Unicorn
listings.content: Pub with a Theatre

listings.name: Neighbour
listings.content: with Jukes Basement Bar: previously the Kentish Town police cells

listings.name: The Oxford Tavern
listings.content: Gastropub

listings.name: The Euston Tap
listings.content: in a classical Victorian Gatehouse

listings.name: The Prince Arthur
listings.content: A nice pub away close to Euston station.

listings.name: The Rocket
listings.address: 120 Euston Rd, Somers Town, London NW1 2AL

listings.name: Scala
listings.content: Former cinema which was used in WWII to manufacture weapons and then faced a piracy lawsuit after screening A Clockwork Orange after Stanley Kubrick famously banned it. Now an alternative music venue.

listings.name: Electric Ballroom
listings.content: A historic ballroom turned contemporary rock music venue. As a former dancefloor, the audience stands on a flat surface so it may be difficult to see the stage further back. The Ballroom hosts several different club nights. It is a big venue with two separate dance floors and four bars. Features a rock floor, as well as a floor for the industrial/goth/rock/techno genres.

listings.name: The Underworld
listings.content: It is a great spot to go and catch alternative bands: goth, metal, electronica, rock, punk and many others are found here. Friday nights are also regular club nights, attracting large numbers from the young alternative crowd and more "studenty" than on Saturdays.

listings.name: KOKO
listings.content: Grade II listed music venue with restaurant. Card only.

listings.name: Smart Camden Inn Hostel
listings.content: Part of the Smart Backpackers chain of hostels, on the street next to Camden High Street.

listings.name: St Christopher's Camden Hostel
listings.content: On the corner of Camden High St and Plender St, which is home to a small morning market. Belushi's bar on the ground floor.
listings.price: Dormitory from £12 which includes breakfast and WiFi

listings.name: Holiday Inn London - Camden Lock
listings.content: A modern hotel with 130 rooms beside the canal at Camden Lock.

listings.name: Premier Inn London King's Cross
listings.content: A modern, clean, reasonably priced hotel.

listings.name: Pullman London St. Pancras
listings.content: It is equidistant from the St. Pancras and Euston railway stations. This former corporate Novotel was taken over and completely refurbished by Accor's upscale Pullman brand. It features rather spacious rooms and interesting views from upper floors, as well as modern decor and fitments and all the creature comforts expected from an upscale hotel.
listings.price: £200 gets you a room with breakfast on most days

listings.name: St. Pancras Renaissance Hotel
listings.content: This is the rebirth of the former Midland Hotel that operated the space from 1873-1935, inside the palatial heritage-listed Neo-Gothic St. Pancras station building above. Definitely outside the budget of many travellers, but for architectural aficionados this is one hotel that should be stayed in at least once in a lifetime. While the public spaces are original, the rooms are in a wing constructed in the 2000s, with the original hotel rooms now being private apartments.

listings.name: Great Northern Hotel
listings.content: The railway hotel of King's Cross station, and the oldest of London's railway hotels, opened in 1854. The hotel is named after the Great Northern Railway, the company that built King's Cross station and operated it until 1923.

listings.name: Bank of England
listings.content: See also: Bank of England Museum.

listings.name: Mansion House
listings.content: Official residence of the Lord Mayor of the City of London, completed in 1753.

listings.name: Monument
listings.content: Designed by Sir Christopher Wren, this tall column (which can be ascended to get a great view) marks the alleged site where the Great Fire of London broke out in September 1666.
listings.price: Adults £4.50, children (5-15) £2.30, students and seniors (60+) £3.00; joint tickets for Tower Bridge and the Monument: adults £11.00, children £5.00, students and seniors £7.50

listings.name: St Giles-without-Cripplegate
listings.content: Medieval Grade I listed church. This church played a key role in the English Revolution and was the parish church of some of the most decisive Puritans: Oliver Cromwell was married and this is where John Milton was buried. It was the home of the Morning Exercises. The tower remains from the original building; the rest was destroyed in the Blitz but rebuilt based on the original plans.

listings.name: St Sepulchre-without-Newgate
listings.content: Grade I listed Saxon church founded before the 12th century. The exterior was mostly constructed in the 15th century, and the interior in the 19th. The north side of the church houses a musician's chapel opened in 1955. In addition to the services, there are often evening (chargeable) concerts.

listings.name: Old Bailey
listings.content: This is probably the most famous criminal court in the world, and has been London's principal criminal court for centuries. It hears cases remitted to it from all over England and Wales as well as the Greater London area. The present building dates largely from 1907 (a new block was added from 1970 for more modern facilities) and stands on the site of the infamous medieval Newgate Gaol. The Central Criminal Court is of course best known today for its association with John Mortimer's Rumpole of the Bailey character, novels and television series. Daily case listings are available at The law pages. No bags, cameras, drinks, food or mobile phones—no facilities for safekeeping. Children under 14 are not admitted.

listings.name: St Paul's Cathedral
listings.content: The great domed cathedral of St Paul's, designed by Sir Christopher Wren to replace the Gothic medieval cathedral destroyed in 1666 in the Great Fire of London, was built between 1675–1710. Of the most famous London sights, St Paul's is the one most conveniently located for the Barbican. It's a significant building in British history, having been the site of the funerals of several British military leaders (Nelson, Wellington, Churchill), and significantly held peace services marking the end of the two world wars. The cathedral is also famous for its Whispering Wall, as well as its stunning view over the city. The crypt is also open to the public, holding the tombs of Nelson, Wellington and Christopher Wren. It is possible to sidestep the admission charge by entering for one of the midday services, even if you don't take part, or for the daily choral evensong in the late afternoon. However, you'd still need a ticket to get to the top. Photography is not allowed.

listings.name: Tower Bridge
listings.content: Magnificent 19th-century bridge, decorated with high towers and featuring a drawbridge. The bridge opens several times each day to permit ships to pass through – timings are dependent on demand, and are not regularly scheduled. When Tower Bridge was built, the area to the west of it was a bustling port – necessitating a bridge that could permit tall boats to pass. Now the South Bank area sits to its west, and the regenerated Butler's Wharf area of shops and riverside restaurants lie to its east. You can get the lift to the top level of the bridge and admire the view. Glass floors provide an interesting perspective for the brave. The museum highlights the bridge's history and engineering, and there are photographic exhibitions along the walkways between the towers.
listings.price: Bridge free; exhibition: adult £9.80, child (5–15) £4.20, senior/student £6.80; joint tickets for exhibition and the Monument: adults £11.00, children £5.00, students and seniors £7.50

listings.name: Tower of London
listings.content: Founded by William the Conqueror in 1066, enlarged and modified by successive sovereigns, the Tower is today one of the world's most famous and spectacular fortresses and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Discover its 900-year history as a royal palace and fortress, prison and place of execution, mint, arsenal, menagerie and jewel house. In the winter you can skate on the dry moat. The Tower contains enough buildings and exhibits to keep a family busy for a full day, with plenty of both warlike and domestic contents. Some areas, such as the St John's Chapel in the White Tower, do not allow photography, but these are clearly signposted. Beefeaters, who are all retired sergeant majors from the British Army, provide guided tours for free as well as ceremonial security. See history come alive – go to the Ceremony of the Keys at the Tower of London. This ceremony, the locking up of the Tower, has been performed every night at 10PM for 800 years. Tickets for the ceremony are £5 and must be prebooked.
listings.price: from £35.80, aged 5-17 £17.90, concession £28.50, entrance with gift aid is about 10% more.. If visiting multiple times or also visiting other Historic Royal Palaces it can be cheaper to buy an HRP annual membership

listings.name: All Hallows by the Tower
listings.content: The oldest church in the City, founded by Saxon abbots in 675 AD.
listings.image: EH1064671 Church of All Hallows by the Tower 07.jpg

listings.name: St Bartholomew-the-Great
listings.content: Founded in 1123, by jester-turned-monk Rahere, this Norman church is one of the oldest in London. It was damaged in the Dissolution but managed to escape both the Great Fire and the Blitz. This is a Grade I listed building. Tourists are welcome when services are not in progress and are charged an admission fee (which does not apply to those coming to pray or use the café).

listings.name: St Botolph's Aldersgate
listings.content: A medieval church that was rebuilt in the late 18th century, noted for its well-preserved interior. The former churchyard was converted into a public space in 1880, called Postman's Park as it was frequented by workers from the nearby Post Office headquarters.

listings.name: Postman's Park
listings.content: Postman's Park is three parks combined, bringing together the gardens of St Botolph's Aldersgate, Christ Church Greyfriars and St Leonard, Foster Lane. One of the largest parks in the City of London, Postman's Park contains the Memorial to Heroic Self Sacrifice; a memorial to ordinary people who died saving the lives of others and might otherwise have been forgotten.

listings.name: St Lawrence Jewry
listings.content: Properly St Lawrence Jewry next Guildhall, it is the official church of the Lord Mayor of London.

listings.name: St Magnus the Martyr
listings.content: Su Catholic Church of England with bells and smells (incense). There is an impressive model of the old London Bridge.

listings.name: St Margaret Pattens
listings.image: St Margaret Pattens, Eastcheap, London EC3 - geograph.org.uk - 1077034.jpg

listings.name: St Mary-at-Hill
listings.image: St Mary at Hill, St Mary at Hill, Cheapside, London EC3 - geograph.org.uk - 717975.jpg

listings.name: St Stephen Walbrook
listings.content: Constructed 1672-9 to a design by Sir Christopher Wren and regarded as one of the finest Wren churches. The 63 feet (19 m) high dome is based on Wren's original design for St Paul's Cathedral. The circular altar is by the British sculptor Henry Moore, and the kneelers are designed by Patrick Heron. Free lunchtime concerts at 1PM on Tuesdays (except August). Free Organ recitals at 12:30PM on Fridays. Occasional art exhibitions on Christian themes and other events.

listings.name: Temple Church
listings.content: A small realm of serenity in the midst of the typical turmoil. It used to be the court of the Knights Templar. You can still visit the beautiful Romanesque church, which is one of the oldest ones in London (opened in 1185) and has connections to the order of Templars. The chancel of the church was built by Henry III. The church still serves the members of Gray's Inn and Lincoln's Inn and has frequent services open to the public. Fans of Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code will recognise the church from both the novel and the film.

listings.name: St Dunstan in the East
listings.content: The ruins of a church dating back to Saxon times, rebuilt by St Dunstan in 950, destroyed in the Great Fire of London, and then rebuilt by Sir Christopher Wren in 1697. Most of the church was destroyed during the blitz, leaving only the tower (dating from Wren's time) and hollowed-out walls (from an 1817 reconstruction). The ruins are now overgrown with picturesque vines and trees, and were converted into a public garden in 1967, complete with benches.

listings.name: Museum of London
listings.content: Now permanently closed, will be replaced by new museum at the former Smithfield market site in 2026. The Museum of London Docklands remains open.
listings.address: London Wall (NB: this is a street!)

listings.name: Guildhall Art Gallery and Roman Amphitheatre
listings.content: The Guildhall Art Gallery houses the City Corporation's art collection, and also runs special exhibitions throughout the year. During construction of the modern gallery, workers discovered the ruins of London's Roman amphitheatre. The gallery was redesigned, and now the Amphitheatre is open to the public within the Guildhall Art Gallery itself and also free of charge.

listings.name: Dr Johnson's House
listings.content: Dr Samuel Johnson was the highly distinguished 18th-century "man of letters", best known for his comprehensive English Dictionary of 1755, but also for his prolific output of poems, essays and novels. Something of a "hidden gem", this small, independent museum is dedicated to him—and, with its historic interiors, paintings and prints, personal effects and other exhibits—gives an impression of what it might have been like during his occupancy from 1748 to 1759. Built in 1700, this impressive period building—a rare example of its kind in the area—survived the brutal onslaught of the Blitz during World War II and is now maintained in excellent condition.
listings.price: adult £4.50, concession £3.50 (over 60, student or registered unemployed), child £1.50 (ages 5-17), family £10 (two adults and accompanying children), under 5s free. No debit or credit cards. National Trust Partner.

listings.name: Bank of England Museum
listings.content: Charts the history of the bank from 1694 to the present day. A highlight is the opportunity to handle a genuine bar of gold. Photography allowed, but no flash.

listings.name: Barbican Centre
listings.content: The largest arts centre in Europe, with music and theatre venues, and changing exhibitions.

listings.name: London Mithraeum
listings.content: The London Mithraeum is a 3rd-century Roman mithraeum that was discovered in Walbrook during construction work in 1954. The entire site was relocated several times before being returned to its original site as part of the new Bloomberg building. This temple of the mystery god Mithras became perhaps the most famous 20th-century Roman discovery in London. In addition to the temple structure, there is a display of Roman artefacts found on the site and a contemporary art exhibit responding to the site. Visitor numbers are limited and timed slots are often fully booked up several weeks in advance, so plan well ahead.
listings.image: Ruins of the Mithras Temple in the City of London, 2004.jpg

listings.name: Barts Pathology Museum
listings.content: Quirky medical museum. Only open to the public for scheduled evening events.

listings.name: Barbican Conservatory
listings.content: The second biggest greenhouse in London, containing over 2,000 species of tropical plants as well as birds and fish.

listings.name: Blitz Plaque
listings.content: The first of tens of thousands of bombs to hit London in World War II fell here in 1940.

listings.name: Baltic Exchange
listings.content: The world's main marketplace for ship broking.

listings.name: London Wall
listings.content: Remains of the wall that surrounded the City of London for almost two thousand years. The parts around the Barbican are mostly Tudor due to maintenance (Roman remains can be seen in and around the Tower of London). Other local remains are the and the name=St Alphage Gdns wall fragment type=see lat=51.5177 long=-0.0922 image=.
listings.image: London Wall bastion, Barber Surgeons' Hall Gardens, London EC2.jpg

listings.name: Lloyds of London
listings.content: The headquarters of world's most famous insurance market, housed in a revolutionary (at the time) bizarre, Matrix-like glass-and-steel building designed by Richard Rogers, with all support services (lifts, ventilation, etc.) suspended outside. Recognised as a masterpiece of exoskeleton architecture.

listings.name: London Stock Exchange
listings.content: After leaving its brutalist skyscraper on Old Broad St, the London Stock Exchange now resides on Paternoster Sq. Dating back to 1698, it is one of the world's oldest and largest stock markets.

listings.name: London Bullion Market Association
listings.content: This is where the world gold price is set twice a day.

listings.name: London Metal Exchange
listings.content: The LME is the leading centre for non-ferrous metals trading. It is also the last financial market in London which still retains open outcry trading.

listings.name: London Stone
listings.content: London Stone is a historic landmark housed in a public display case at 111 Cannon Street in the City of London. It is an irregular block of oolitic limestone measuring 53 × 43 × 30 cm (21″ × 17″ × 12″), the remnant of a once much larger object that had stood for many centuries on the south side of the street.

listings.name: St Bride Printing Library
listings.content: This specialist small library houses an impressive range of books on graphic design, typography, bookbinding and papermaking. The books cannot be borrowed but can be photocopied or photographed (with permission). An essential visit for any graphic design student.

listings.name: The Gherkin
listings.content: Designed by one of Britain's leading architects, Sir Norman Foster, this curved glass skyscraper was the 2004 recipient of the Stirling Architectural Prize for Best Building. It was built on the site of the Baltic Exchange building, destroyed in 1992 by an IRA bomb which killed three. On the Bury Street side of the Gherkin by some black stone benches is the Tomb of the Unknown Girl for a teenaged Londoner who died 1,600 years ago (see infobox above), marked with a marble laurel wreath and inscription. Searcy's Restaurant (from £50) at the top takes bookings up to five weeks in advance and you have to go through security before going up.
listings.price: No entry, unless you have a restaurant reservation. Free to stand outside

listings.name: Willis Building
listings.content: Completed in 2008 opposite Lloyd's of London.

listings.name: Leadenhall Building
listings.content: Another Richard Rogers creation, nicknamed the Cheesegrater. Completed in 2014. Also opposite Lloyd's.

listings.name: 20 Fenchurch Street
listings.content: The unusual "walkie scorchie" profile of this skyscraper by Rafael Vinoly has seen it grab the headlines, as did the "death rays" caused by the sun's heat reflecting off the building onto the street below when it was first completed; car tyres melted and burst, and at least one man fried an egg using only the heat from the walkie talkie. Visitors can access the sky garden to see a magnificent view over the City and beyond; it's the only place you can't see the tower from! Online booking to visit during the day is essential. Alternatively, you can eat at one of the restaurants in the evening.

listings.name: Fishmongers' Hall
listings.content: The main headquarters of the Worshipful Company of Fishmongers and a Grade II* listed building.

listings.name: Horizon 22
listings.content: London's highest viewing platform that is free to the public. Sitting at the 58th floor of an office building, and the tallest building in City of London proper, it gives visitors a 300-degree view of London.

listings.name: Barbican Architecture Tour
listings.content: 90-minute tour of the beautifully ugly brutalist site.

listings.name: Gresham College
listings.content: Founded in 1597 as London's alternative higher education institution to Oxford and Cambridge, Gresham College continues to provide free public lectures every week during term time. Most lectures require no booking, with wonderful speakers delivering lectures on a wide range of interesting topics.

listings.name: Lord Mayor's Show
listings.content: The ceremony celebrates the appointment of the new Lord Mayor of the City of London. It is one of the great annual processions held in all London.

listings.name: London Walks
listings.content: Consider going along on one of the many excellent guided tours of the City, often with an evocative theme for example ghosts or Jack the Ripper.

listings.name: London Night Tour
listings.address: Departing from Coach stop 3, Bulleid Way

listings.name: Assenheims 56
listings.content: South American cuisine

listings.name: Pilpel
listings.content: A falafel restaurant.

listings.name: Eataly London
listings.content: An Italian food hall and eatery opened in 2021 along the lines of the Turin original. It's east side of Liverpool St station.

listings.name: Polo Bar
listings.content: An unpretentious cafe serving fried breakfasts and similar basic food 24 hr a day, and a great place for a late snack after you leave the Eat & Drink. Liverpool St is a safe area anyway but you cannot get safer than this for a late night meal, as at night you'll often see police from the nearby City of London police station. There are no toilets, however, so you need to use those at nearby Liverpool St Station.

listings.name: Smiths of Smithfields
listings.content: Smiths of Smithfield is a Grade II listed four-floor restaurant serving great British food.

listings.name: Wood Street Bar and Restaurant
listings.content: Real ale, nice food and a relaxed atmosphere.
listings.image: Wood Street Bar and Restaurant, Barbican, EC2 (4160060518).jpg

listings.name: Apulia
listings.content: Italian restaurant.

listings.name: Duck and Waffle
listings.content: All day dining on the 40th floor of the Heron Tower. Popular in the very late night for a bite after going out and waiting to watch the sunrise over the rest of London.

listings.name: Angler
listings.content: One Michelin-starred British seafood restaurant with views over the City.
listings.price: Tasting menu £100 / £170 with wine pairing. À la carte mains £24-£30 (April 2021)

listings.name: Hand & Shears
listings.content: Grade II listed historic pub

listings.name: The Hope
listings.content: Grade II listed pub

listings.name: The Jugged Hare
listings.content: A gastropub modelled on a traditional countryside drinking establishment, with a hunting theme. The tables are actually old whisky barrels and the décor features several stuffed animals and trophies. Completing the pattern, the food is heavily game-based, with some seafood. Their titular signature dish is an 18th-century stew recipe.

listings.name: Old Red Cow
listings.content: Small pub that serves real ale and craft beer from both major and local breweries.

listings.name: Dirty Dick's
listings.content: One of the better known pubs (although definitely no tourist trap) near Liverpool St, supposedly named after a Georgian dandy who let himself go on the death of his fiancée.

listings.name: The Old Doctor Butler's Head
listings.content: This claims to be one of London's oldest pubs, tracing it history to 1610, although it has been rebuilt since then. The eponymous Doctor Butler was a purveyor of "medicinal ale" who was appointed court physician to James I. Pubs selling his beer were allowed to display his portrait, hence the name of the establishment.

listings.name: The Crosse Keys
listings.content: Part of the JD Wetherspoons chain in a converted bank. As is usual for the chain, it is fairly cheap with decent food and drink. The ex-bank building makes this pub a little grander and more spacious than most.

listings.name: The Hung Drawn & Quartered
listings.content: Fullers Pub

listings.name: Lamb Tavern
listings.content: One of several pubs in Leadenhall Market where you can listen to insurance brokers from nearby Lloyd's talk business.

listings.name: The Ship
listings.content: A Nicolson's pub rebuilt after it was burnt down during the fire of London.

listings.name: The Sterling
listings.content: A central bar that resides in the heart of the Gherkin. Catch your breath from the bustle of the City and enjoy a bit of al fresco dining. Food and drink available.

listings.name: The Blackfriar
listings.content: A pub with an art deco church built inside.

listings.name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
listings.content: An old City pub establishment, rebuilt shortly after the Great Fire of 1666. All the monarchs who have reigned in England during the pub's time are written by the main door.

listings.name: The Sugar Loaf
listings.content: Pub that is popular with City workers. You will often find a crowd spilling out into the adjacent pedestrian area, particularly on Tuesdays-Thursdays when workers tend to come into the office more.

listings.name: Savage Garden
listings.content: Cocktail bar with 360 views of London

listings.name: Vinoteca
listings.content: Wine bar and shop.

listings.name: Fabric
listings.content: A massive club (think cathedral scale) that provides a more underground version of Ministry of Sound and hosts some of the biggest names in dance music, from Goldie to David Holmes to the Scratch Perverts. There are always big queues, so get down early if you can.

listings.name: The Hoxton, Shoreditch
listings.content: 210 room hotel, with some cheaper "shoebox" rooms.

listings.name: YHA London St Paul's
listings.content: Small hostel converted from one of the City's oldest buildings. Cheap for Central London accommodation, range of room sizes, basic facilities.
listings.price: Dorm from £18.95 including breakfast. 6 rooms for 2 people and 3 singles

listings.name: Apex City of London Hotel
listings.content: Located in the City close to the Tower of London. 179 luxury bedrooms and suites, restaurant, bar and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

listings.name: Apex Temple Court Hotel
listings.content: 184 spacious luxury bedrooms and suites, bar, restaurant, executive lounge and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

listings.name: Queen Street St Paul's Apartments
listings.content: These serviced apartments are situated in the centre of the City area of London, with Walbrook, Bank and Monument being a short walk away. The neighbouring streets are filled with cafes, restaurants and local shops, ensuring your stay is both enjoyable and convenient.

listings.name: Apex London Wall Hotel
listings.content: Close to the Bank of England and Liverpool Street Station. 89 luxury bedrooms and suites, bar, restaurant and gym. Free fast speed Wi-fi.

listings.name: Andaz London Liverpool Street
listings.content: A concept casual luxury hotel. No two bedrooms the same.

listings.name: SACO Apartments – Aldgate
listings.content: A grade II listed Victorian building. A great alternative to hotels for those travelling on business.

listings.name: CitizenM Tower of London
listings.content: Slick modern hotel, try for a room with a view of Tower of London. No dogs.

listings.name: Citadines Holborn-Covent Garden London
listings.content: Located a short walk from Covent Garden. Each air-conditioned apartment houses a bathroom with a separate toilet, a separate kitchen area and Internet access.

listings.name: Malmaison London
listings.content: Great location with attentive staff.

listings.name: South Place Hotel
listings.content: Chic city hotel with good grub in the Chop House and great dining in the Angler's Restaurant.
